title: Grace at meals
hook: bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts

segments.voice: Yesterday, name days, and a phone that buzzed all morning for Saint Nicholas. Your line was your name has a story. Whose name story did you hear? Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

"Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts." At one kitchen table, a family says it so fast it comes out as a single long word, and the youngest is reaching for the potatoes before the amen. At another table, an old couple hold hands across the plates and say it slowly, the way they've said it for years. In a school cafeteria, a girl bows her head for two seconds over a tray, and nobody notices but her. The words are short. The food is getting cold. And still, in homes all over, people stop, just before the first bite. Today: grace at meals.

Start with the words themselves. The old Catholic grace goes: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." Look at what it calls the food. Not dinner. Gifts. Before anyone has tasted it, the meal has been named as something given. Other churches have their own graces, rhymed or spoken freely, but they tend to do the same thing. Next, Jesus at a meal. In Mark's Gospel a hungry crowd sits on the grass, and there's almost nothing to eat. The disciples want to send everyone away to buy food. Instead, Jesus takes what there is, and Mark says: "he looked up to heaven, and blessed, and brake the loaves." Look up, bless, break. That's the shape of grace: a pause, a word of thanks, and then the food is shared. Then, an older command. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee." Notice when: after the meal, when you're full, which is exactly when it's easiest to forget. Jewish tradition keeps a blessing after eating from this verse. Christian graces come before the meal, after it, or both. Last, a line from Paul's letter to Timothy: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Thanksgiving turns an ordinary plate into a received gift. That's what the old grace is doing in its short, fast way. It doesn't change the food. It changes how the food is received: these thy gifts.
screen: `BLESS US, O LORD, AND THESE THY GIFTS.`
`HE LOOKED UP, AND BLESSED, AND BRAKE.`
`WHEN THOU HAST EATEN AND ART FULL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say grace before eating. If there's food or a drink near you, set it in front of you. If not, bring your next meal to mind. Settle, and breathe. Look at what's there and trace it backward: the hands that cooked it, the store, the truck, the field, the rain. Let each step take a breath. If you pray, you can say the old grace slowly, one phrase at a time: bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts. If you don't, simply name, silently, a few of the people it took to bring this food to you. The bell holds the time.

segments.voice: Grace at meals. A short pause of thanks before or after eating, naming the food as a gift and God as the giver.
Your line: these thy gifts. Today, before one meal or snack, stop for the length of a single breath before the first bite. Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Christians of different churches say a short grace before meals, at home or in public; Catholics often use "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts," others use their own set words or pray in their own words, and some also give thanks after eating.
